newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian markets expected to remain on edge in week ahead.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets expected to remain on edge in week ahead.

text.p: - Asian markets were expected to remain on edge in the week ahead, with Hong Kong, Australia and Manila worried about prospects for a U.S. interest rate hike and Tokyo about domestic economic troubles.

Expectations were more positive for Bangkok and Seoul, where shares should be bouyed by foreign bargain hunting, and for Dhaka, where government pronouncements on privatisation should act as a boost. Shares should be mixed for other Asian markets.

After a rough week, Wall Street should be looking forward to the Labour Day holiday on Monday. Blue-chip stocks fell sharply on Friday after unexpectedly strong data reinforced fears that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates to head off inflation as the economy continues to grow.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 31.44 points at 5,616.21. For the week, the index lost 106.53 points, the most since May.
TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market's key Nikkei average is seen likely to extend losses towards the key 20,000 level following its tumble by nearly two percent on Friday.
"The investment environment is bad," said Keiji Arai, a strategist at Sanyo Securities Co Ltd.
"The outlook for the economy is gloomy, while the market is weighed down by a slew of new stock issues," Arai said.
Brokers said that, given the number of negative factors, the Nikkei average could breach the 20,000 level at any time.
On Friday, the key 225-share Nikkei average slid 386.26 points or 1.88 percent to close at 20,166.90.

HONG KONG - Stocks are expected to search for support in the week ahead, after renewed fears of rising interest rates pushed the Hang Seng index down through key support levels on Friday, analysts said.
The Hang Seng index tumbled 169.19 points on Friday, falling through support at about 11,200 points to end at 11,159.02. Over the week it shed 266 points, or 2.32 percent.
"I think it will still be looking for a bottom level," said Boby Ho, dealing manager at GK Goh Securities. He said 11,000 was an important support level.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected in a firming trend in the week ahead as Morgan Stanley was scheduled to include Taiwan into its global indices from September 2, brokers said.

"Most analysts so far still expect a gradual upward trend, although foreign funds are not necessarily to actively enter because of a slowing economy currently," said Eric Liu of National Securities. "We'll also have to watch any new development between Taiwan and China and whether new bellwether shares may emerge," Liu said.
Institutional investors, including local and foreign funds, have been consecutive net buyers recently because they expected more foreign fund inflows on Morgan Stanley move, brokers said.
On Saturday, the index ended at 6,324.60 points, compared with 6,190.56 a week earlier. A 6,250-6,450 range was seen for next week.

BANGKOK - The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index is expected to rise on expectations of high liquidity in the money market and on bargain-hunting by foreign investors after recent stock price drops, brokers said.

"Liquidity in the system is expected to be high (in the coming) week and that should boost buying sentiment. Foreigners are also expected to continue buying from this week," said Thanadech Mahapokai of Book Club Finance and Securities.
The SET index closed at 1,102.32 on Friday, compared with 1,106.73 last Friday.

KUALA LUMPUR - Narrow-ranged, easier trading seen in Kuala Lumpur blue chips should continue while small-capitalisation stocks, which shot to record levels this week, could take a breather next week, dealers said.
The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index of Malaysia's 100 biggest firms ended on Friday at 1,118.57, up 8.08 points, down 0.83 points from the previous week.
"There's quite a lack of interest, so I think chances are that it will erode a bit more," said a market analyst with a local research firm.
The Second Board index closed at a record of 541.75 on Wednesday, its third all-time high in a row this week.
"I think there will be profit-taking," said William Chan, an institutional dealer with Seagroatt and Campbell.
MANILA - The expected good news on first half Gross National Product and the August inflation rate could help the Manila market break out of its tight range, analysts said.
The GNP data is scheduled for release on Monday and inflation data on Thursday.

Fears of a hike in U.S. interest rates could dampen the market, Ramon Lucas of Rashid Hussain Securities said, adding: "The market may shrug off the overseas concerns when local investors buy up on the GNP and inflation news."
Over the week, the main index dropped 5.75 points week-on-week to 3,220.71 points after investors cashed in on recent gains.
SEOUL - Shares are expected to climb early in the coming week on bargain hunting by domestic institutions and foreign investors, brokers said.
However, the 800 level was seen as a strong resistance line, and selling at that level could send the composite stock index sliding back down, they said.
"I didn't expect to see the recent rebound come so fast," said a Schroders broker. "I think 800 is the upper limit for now because economic fundamentals haven't changed."
On Friday, the composite index closed at 782.87, up 1.45 points or 0.19 percent, from last Friday's closing of 781.42.
SINGAPORE - Dealers said trading in Singapore shares should perform better on a technical rebound after a week of dull trade.
They said a strong Malaysian National Day rally might push up the Malaysian over-the-counter stocks traded in Singapore. Malaysia celebrates its National Day on Saturday.
On Friday, the key Straits Times Industrials Index was 2,153.54, down 27.98 points from last Friday's 2,181.52.
SYDNEY - The Australian share market outlook is seen as mixed to weaker in the near term with the tone expected to be set by Wall Street as U.S. bonds continue to suffer from rate tightening fears.
The benchmark All Ordinaries finished at 2,268.7, down 24.2 points over the week.
With profit results driving individual stocks, the broader market suffered from a flow-on of Wall Street's weakness.
"People are very jittery on the outlook for bonds and they are keeping a close eye on them," said Peter Struk, a dealer at brokerage Reynolds and Co.
JAKARTA - Jakarta share prices were likely to be mixed in the coming week as many brokers were waiting for positive news to stimulate fresh buying.

"Many operators are likely to re-enter the market as prevailing share prices are quite cheap. They are just waiting for better market sentiment," Pungky Kuntjaraningrat, research analyst for Pentasena Securities.
Brokers said the ongoing court case involving the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) could also keep some foreign investors on the sidelines.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed down 2.42 points, or 0.44 percent to close at 547.61 points, against last week's close of 549.21 points.
BOMBAY - Indian stocks will be guided in the coming week by what relief the government plans to give to industry and small investors, brokers said.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram will address parliament on Monday about the proposed 1996/97 (April-March) budget, beginning a weeklong debate on the finance bill. The market expects changes to a controversial tax proposal.
"We're cautiously optimistic," said one trader.
The expectations drove the 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index up 21 points, or 0.60 percent, to close at 3,514.61 on Friday.
COLOMBO - Shares are expected to stay range-bound with interest focused on plantation firms being privatised and a handful of other selected stocks on lack of liquidity, brokers said.
"There is buying interest among stocks with attractive profit prospects, but the problem is to source shares," said a trader at brokerage Lanka Securities.

Sellers have retreated to the sidelines awaiting further rises in the index after signs of strong support around the 550-level, brokers said. The index closed at 559.23 on Friday, little changed from 556.30 a week earlier.
